docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of this individual block diagram is to showcse the hardware architecture, electrical interfaces, and signal flow for the Servo Motor Subsystem of Team's Modular Spider Leg.

Key system parameters: * Power Source & Levels: The board is powered by an external 9V DC wall adapter, which is stepped down via a linear regulator (LM7805) to a regulated 5V DC supply. This 5V domain powers the servo motor and the microcontroller. * Actuator & Sensors: The primary actuator is a standard servo motor (e.g., TowerPro SG90) driven by a 5V PWM signal directly from the microcontroller. * Team Connections: Operating as a "spoke" in our team's hub-and-spoke method, this board connects to the main hub board using the standard 8-pin ribbon connector. * Signal Flow: The central hub sends digital position commands via a serial connection on Pin 1 to the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller's UART RX pin. The microcontroller translates this command and outputs a digital parallel PWM signal to drive the servo motor to the target angle.

docs.title: Driver Nano 1 (Servo + Display)
docs.text:
This page covers the components for Driver Nano 1: the joint-1 servo and the diagnostic display. Driver Nano 1 receives target positions from the Main Processor Nano over the I2C, drives the joint, shows leg status on the display, and reports status back.

Selection criteria used for both components

  • Runs from the 5 V logic domain used by the Nano.
  • Has a manufacturer or available datasheet.
  • Uses few Nano pins and little RAM.
  • Does not use the Nano's hardware I2C pins (A4/A5), which are reserved for the command bus to the Main Nano.

Hip Joint Servo (Rotary Actuator)

  1. Hitec HS-485HB standard analog servo

    • $28.99/each
    • HS-485HB product page at Amzaon
    • HS-485HB manufacturer datasheet
    Pros Cons Position control is built in: the internal potentiometer holds the commanded angle, so the Nano only outputs one 50 Hz PWM signal (Servo library, any digital pin) and no driver IC is needed. Stall current is 1.0 A at 4.8 V and 1.2 A at 6 V per the datasheet, so the regulator and wiring must be sized for it, and the servo cannot be powered from the Nano's 5V pin or USB. Stall torque of 4.8 kgf·cm at 4.8 V and 6.0 kgf·cm at 6 V in a 45 g package gives the highest torque per gram of the three options. Karbonite (plastic) gears can strip under shock loads such as a leg strike, and metal-gear servos cost more. It runs from the same 4.8–6 V range as the logic, and the manufacturer datasheet lists stall current, idle current, speed, and dimensions, which makes the power budget straightforward. The servo gives no position output, so the Nano cannot confirm that the joint reached the angle. The status sent to the Main Nano is the commanded value, not a measured one.

  2. NEMA 17 bipolar stepper (17HS15-1704S) with DRV8825 stepper driver carrier

    • Motor: $9.98
    • 17HS4023S Stepper motor product page at Amazon
    • 17HS15-1704S full datasheet

    • Driver: $15.95
    • DRV8825 driver product page at Pololu
    • DRV8825 datasheet (Texas Instruments)
    Pros Cons The motor's rated current of about 0.7 A per phase is well under the DRV8825 carrier's roughly 1.5 A limit without a heat sink, so no extra cooling is needed. Holding torque is only about 14 N·cm (roughly 1.4 kgf·cm), about a third of the HS-485HB's 4.8 kgf·cm at 4.8 V, so a gearbox would likely be needed for a hip joint, adding cost, backlash, and mass. The DRV8825 provides up to 1/32 microstepping from a 1.8° step motor, and the Nano only has to output STEP and DIR pulses with no PWM timing constraints. The DRV8825 needs an 8.2–45 V motor supply (the motor is rated for 12 V), so it cannot run from the 5–6 V logic rail and adds a second power rail, regulator, and power budget line. The shaft holds position while the coils are energized with no gear train to strip, and the DRV8825 adds over-current protection, thermal shutdown, and an adjustable current limit. It is open loop with no position feedback, so lost steps go undetected and the joint needs a homing switch at power-up, and the coils draw current continuously while holding.

Choice: Option 1: Hitec HS-485HB standard servo

Reason: The HS-485HB is the best match for the Driver Nano 1 architecture. Its internal closed-loop position control means the Nano only needs one PWM pin and the standard Servo library, and it runs from the same 4.8–6 V supply as the rest of the subsystem. The stepper option (Option 2) is the most inexpensive motor, but the DRV8825 needs at least 8.2 V, which forces a second power rail and regulator, and the 280 g motor is about six times heavier than the servo for similar torque.

Diagnostic Display (leg status)

  1. 2.42 inches 128x64 IIC I2C OLED Display Module (Amazon)

    • Price: $15.59
    • 2.42 Inches I2C OLED Display Module on Amazon
    • Oled Display Datasheet
    Pros Cons Large 2.42-inch, 128×64 display provides clear text and enough space for angles, status, and fault messages. The SSD1309 controller requires a compatible library and may not work correctly with every SSD1306 example. Uses only four I²C connections: VCC, GND, SDA, and SCL. It is larger and more expensive than common 0.96-inch OLED modules. Supports 3–5 V power and provides bright, high-contrast graphics without a backlight. Static images displayed for long periods can cause pixel dimming or burn in.

  2. Adafruit Standard 16×2 character LCD

    • Price: $9.95
    • Adafruit Standard LCD 16×2 (ADA181) product page
    • Adafruit Standard LCD 16×2 Display Code Datasheet
    • Adafruit Standard LCD 16×2 Display Wiring Datasheet
    Pros Cons Adafruit provides a datasheet with pin locations and the HD44780 command-set datasheet. It is text-only (16 characters × 2 rows), so it cannot show graphics or a compact status layout. The single-row 0.1" header suits breadboards and through-hole boards. It needs six Nano digital lines in 4-bit mode (versus two for an I2C OLED). Adding the I2C backpack would reduce the pins but add cost and put it on the I2C bus. The LiquidCrystal library ships with the Arduino IDE and uses very little RAM, so it avoids the OLED frame-buffer issue. A contrast potentiometer and backlight resistor are needed, and the backlight draws current continuously. The blue LED backlight can be dimmed with a resistor or PWM and uses much less power than EL backlights. The module is physically larger than the OLED.

Choice: Option 1: 2.42 inches 128x64 IIC I2C OLED Display Module

Reason: The OLED can show multiple lines of leg status (commanded angle, measured status, fault flags) and simple graphics, which the 16×2 LCD cannot. It needs only two signal pins, whereas the LCD needs six. Using the U8g2 library in page buffer mode on software I2C (pins D4/D5) solves two Nano problems at once: it keeps only about 128 bytes of RAM in use, and it leaves the hardware I2C pins (A4/A5) free as the command bus to the Main Nano.

Pin Table (Potential Pin Connection Plan, Driver Nano 1)

PIC pin Function Connects to RC2 7 Servo PWM output RB2 9 I2C SDA RB1 10 I2C SCL RC4 11 Spare GPIO RC5 12 Spare GPIO RF0 25 UART TX RF1 26 UART RX RF4 34 Debug LED output RF7 37 Debug push-button input VTG 51 Board power input

Peripheral Connector Wiring

Connector Pin Connection J2 Servo 1 Servo PWM signal from RC2 through R1 J2 Servo 2 +5V_SERVO from JP1 J2 Servo 3 Earth J3 OLED 1 Earth J3 OLED 2 Main +5 V J3 OLED 3 I2C SCL from RB1 J3 OLED 4 I2C SDA from RB2 J5 Expansion 1 Earth J5 Expansion 2 RC5 J5 Expansion 3 RC4 J5 Expansion 4 Main +5 V

The HS-485HB servo is powered by a separate LM7805 regulator. Jumper-1 allows the servo supply to be disconnected during testing. The OLED and PIC development board use the main regulated +5 V supply. All other pins have a common Earth connection.
